Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences. ## The competition boundary A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board. For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other. The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time. ## What the game saves today `src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values. An example stored value is: ```json { "schemaVersion": 1, "size": 10, "bestMoves": { "4": 12, --- open-forge: description: Name-length acceptance, Unicode counting units and boundary examples. tags: - Forms - Names - Unicode --- # Name length policy This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits. The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page. ## The checked value The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md). Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width. The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script. A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling. ## Code points, code units and visible text JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points. A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form. The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted. In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper. ## Boundary examples The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist. --- open-forge: description: The leave-work confirmation policy and its boundary with current direct deal actions. tags: - Controls - Dialogs - Policy --- # Dialog policy This page records the confirmation policy for leaving unfinished work and its relationship to the game's existing actions. The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly. ## The confirmation boundary A confirmation is useful only when it corresponds to a real decision about abandoning work. Its content and focus need to make the conservative path understandable before the player commits to leaving. Leaving unfinished work asks first in a native dialog element with two buttons, Keep playing and Leave. Keep playing takes focus when it opens, and Escape keeps playing. The decision is about the unfinished work being left; opening a disclosure to inspect a code is not itself that decision. There is no third action specified by this policy. In particular, the existing snapshot exporter does not turn this confirmation into an automatic save workflow. Export is a separate user action with a text result. A feature that uses the confirmation can draw on that distinction without presenting an unsaved draft as if it had already been preserved. The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement. ## What the present controls actually do `Controls.tsx` renders New Game and Restart as native buttons. Their callbacks in `use-game.ts` reset the clock adapter and commit a replacement game. They do not consult `started`, Moves, Pairs or a dialog result before doing so. The existing game replaces immediately when those buttons are used. BoardCodeForm validates before replacing. Its `loadBoard` callback returns false for invalid input and true after successful replacement. Snapshot loading decodes the whole draft before replacing as well. These paths protect against invalid external data; they are not implementations of a leave confirmation. The native `details` panel is also not a modal. It expands in document flow and leaves the rest of the page operable. Calling its summary a dialog trigger would misdescribe both the DOM and its focus behavior. [Reproduction panel](reproduction-panel.md) documents the actual disclosure. This distinction matters during incremental work. A new dialog in one feature does not silently change the semantics of every old control. When reading a change, follow the event handler to see whether it reaches a confirmation boundary, a parser, or the replacement directly. Similar visual labels do not establish the same lifecycle. ## Native behavior and application decisions --- open-forge: description: Current action focus and board memory, plus the policy for main-screen replacements. tags: - Input - Focus - Policy --- # Focus policy This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen. Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things. ## Existing page and future screens `Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen. A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists. The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus. ## Initial load is quiet The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method. The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board. A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing. ## Deal actions retain their location New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call. --- open-forge: description: Status publication, repeated event identity, turn results and load feedback. tags: - Input - Accessibility - Status --- # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. --- open-forge: description: The result-table markup policy and how it differs from current statistics and cards. tags: - Controls - Semantics - Policy --- # Tables policy This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure. There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented. ## Policy for result data When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning. This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things. No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format. ## Why the statistics are a definition list GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read. The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure. The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen. [Status bar](status-bar.md) documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns. ## Why the card board is not a table --- open-forge: description: The feature JSON envelope and its distinction from the existing versioned preference aggregate. tags: - Persistence - Formats --- # Persistence envelope This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs. The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape. ## The feature value boundary A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection. This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records. The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [Data exchange policy](../sharing/data-exchange-policy.md) when following a value across those boundaries. ## The existing aggregate, precisely The current storage writer does this: ```ts JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences }) ``` `PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example: ```json {"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}} ```

// An independent reading of D03 and D04 in exact BigInt arithmetic, kept apart from the game's deck code.
const MULTIPLIER = 16807n;
const MODULUS = 2147483647n;
const DRAW_RANGE = 2147483646n;

export function specDeal(size: number, seed: number): number[] {
  const deck = Array.from({ length: size * size }, (_, position) => Math.floor(position / 2));
  let state = BigInt(seed);
  for (let index = deck.length - 1; index > 0; index -= 1) {
    const choices = BigInt(index + 1);
    const limit = (DRAW_RANGE / choices) * choices;
    let draw: bigint;
    do {
      state = (state * MULTIPLIER) % MODULUS;
      draw = state - 1n;
    } while (draw >= limit);
    const other = Number(draw % choices);
    const current = deck[index];
    const swapped = deck[other];
    if (current === undefined || swapped === undefined) throw new Error('Deal index out of range.');
    deck[index] = swapped;
    deck[other] = current;
  }
  return deck;
}

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
---

# Input
Input is a set of controls that lets you play Neon Pairs with a pointer, touch or keyboard.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can reveal a card with a tap, then move to its partner with the arrow keys. Every activation uses the same game action, so changing input methods keeps the same turn.

## Activation

The card controls follow these rules:

- I01 - Render each card as a native button. A primary click, a completed tap, Enter and Space activate the card through the same action.
- I03 - Keep the browser's normal context menu on right-click or long-press. Opening that menu doesn't activate a card.
- I04 - Hover and pointer cancellation leave the game state unchanged.

The game decides whether an activation changes a card. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for matches, repeated selections, blocked turns and turn timing.

## Keyboard movement

- I05 - Give the board one remembered tab stop. When Tab enters the board, focus that card. Use the first card before any board focus has been remembered.

- I06 - Move focus with these keys. Movement changes focus without activating a card:

| Key | Focus destination |
| --- | --- |
| ArrowLeft | Previous card in the same row |
| ArrowRight | Next card in the same row |
| ArrowUp | Card in the previous row and same column |
| ArrowDown | Card in the next row and same column |

The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.

- I07 - Stop arrow movement at a board edge. Moving left from the first column keeps focus on the same card.

- I08 - Let native Tab and Shift+Tab leave the board. Moving through the board uses the movement keys instead of adding every card to the page's tab order.

## Focus

The board keeps focus separate from play:

- I09 - Keep matched cards focusable and mark them `aria-disabled="true"`. Their game action follows the matched-card rule in the gameplay document.
- I10 - While a mismatching pair waits to turn back, allow focus movement and block card activation.
- I11 - On initial load, keep the browser's current focus. Loading the game doesn't move focus to the board.
- I12 - After a new deal, Restart or a successful load, reset the board's remembered tab stop to its first card.
- I13 - When a card receives focus, scroll it into view with nearest alignment in the board's scroll area. Give each card a scroll margin of at least 6px, so its complete focus outline stays in view, including mid-board cards.

The session buttons keep their focus as defined in [Controls](controls.md).

## Card names

The button names describe the information available to the player:

- I14 - Name a hidden card by its one-based row, column and closed state. Keep its face SVG and face identifier out of the DOM while it is hidden, including attributes and accessible text.
- I15 - Name a revealed or matched card by its position, face name and state. Use the face names defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).

For example, the first hidden button is named "Row 1, column 1, closed". Once revealed, its name includes the face, so a player can remember it without seeing the drawing.

## Announcements

- I16 - Use one polite, atomic live region for turn results and completion. Announce each turn result exactly once. A winning turn has one announcement containing both the match and the win. Consecutive identical results each get their own announcement. Focus movement, clock renders and closing a mismatch don't repeat a result.

Use these turn announcements, where `M` is the matched pair count, `N` is moves and `time` uses R07's display format:

| Event | Announcement |
| --- | --- |
| First match | Pair found. 1 pair matched. |
| Later match | Pair found. M pairs matched. |
| Miss | No match. Cards close after a short pause. |
| Final match | Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time. |

Send the load statuses in Controls through this same live region once per load event. Keep the visible status beside the reproduction controls.

For example, moving across three cards leaves the current announcement unchanged. Resolving the next pair announces that turn's result.

## Screen reader

- I17 - Support a complete 4x4 keyboard game with a screen reader. Find Grid size and New Game by name, enter the board, expose closed positions and revealed faces by name and state, announce one result per turn and make the win, final moves and time available. Leave the board with Tab and start another game. Deliver automated accessibility-tree evidence for this journey. Record the browser and tool versions in the project README and say whether a screen reader was used. If one was used, record its name and version. The user confirms spoken output during acceptance. Spoken confirmation isn't the developer's deliverable.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
---

# Visuals
Visuals is a design specification that defines the layout, colors and card artwork for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card face combines a shape, a marker position and a fill. You can identify a pair from those features even when you can't distinguish its color.

## Layout

- V01 - Use native controls and a CSS Grid board of DOM card buttons with inline SVG artwork. Render the game without canvas. Use no component library.
- V02 - Center the content within a maximum width of 1120px and give it 16px padding. Keep the outer page within the viewport width.
- V03 - Limit the board's scroll area to `70dvh`, capped at 768px tall. Give it 6px padding and allow overflow on both axes inside that area.
- V04 - Make each card square and size it from 44px to 88px according to the available board width. Use a 6px grid gap, a 2px card border and an 8px card radius.
- V05 - Fit the default four-column board within a phone viewport. When a larger board reaches the 44px minimum card size, keep that size and scroll inside the board.

For example, a sixteen-column board needs 794px for its cards and gaps, plus 12px for board padding. On a phone, the board scrolls while the outer page stays within the viewport width.

The 44px minimum is the chosen card target size. It doesn't state that the complete game conforms to an accessibility standard.

## Colors

- V06 - Use these colors for the page and controls:

| Token | Color | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page | `#090B14` | Page background |
| Panel | `#141827` | Board scroll area, reproduction panel and non-card button, select, input and textarea backgrounds |
| Back | `#1B2034` | Hidden card background |
| Face | `#111625` | Revealed card background |
| Text | `#F4F6FF` | Main text |
| Secondary | `#B8BDD2` | Help text, status labels and optional supporting text |
| Border | `#757C9A` | Neutral borders |
| Focus | `#FFFFFF` | Focus outline |

- V07 - Use this ordered palette for card artwork:

| Index | Name | Color |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Cyan | `#63E7FF` |
| 1 | Magenta | `#FF71D6` |
| 2 | Green | `#8BEA7D` |
| 3 | Yellow | `#FFE082` |
| 4 | Orange | `#FFB064` |
| 5 | Violet | `#B49AFF` |
| 6 | Rose | `#FF8296` |
| 7 | Ice | `#D9F3FF` |

## Type and spacing

- V08 - Use the system sans-serif font stack. Set body text to 16px with a 24px line height, the title to 24px and secondary text to 14px. Secondary text means help text, status labels and optional supporting text.

- V09 - Use spacing values of 4px, 6px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px and 32px for positive layout gaps, padding and margins you set. Allow zero resets and automatic centering. Reset browser default margins. Native control internals aren't covered. Card borders, radii, focus outlines, font metrics and SVG coordinates use their own stated values.

## Card faces

- V10 - Generate 128 face identities from integer face IDs `0` through `127`. Calculate each face from these ordered values:

| Part | Calculation | Ordered values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | `id % 8` | Circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, hexagon, plus, chevron |
| Marker | `floor(id / 8) % 8` | Top, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom, bottom-left, left, top-left |
| Fill | `floor(id / 64)` | Solid, outline |
| Color | Palette at marker index | The eight palette colors above |

- V11 - Treat shape, marker and fill as the face identity. Color repeats the marker distinction and doesn't create a separate identity.

- V12 - Draw each face in an SVG with `viewBox="0 0 100 100"`. Center the main shape within `x=25..75` and `y=25..75`. Draw the marker above the shape as a circle with radius 5, centered 40 units from `(50, 50)` in its marker direction. Give the marker a 3-unit stroke in the Face background color, so it stays separate from the shape. Normalize diagonal directions, giving offsets of about 28.284 units on each axis. Use a 5-unit stroke for an outlined shape. At 44px, all 128 identities must be distinguishable in a grayscale face sheet, including solid and outlined squares with diagonal markers.

Use the face color for the solid shape's fill, the outlined shape's stroke and the marker's fill. An outlined shape has no fill. The marker keeps its Face-background stroke.

- V13 - Name each face with lowercase palette, fill, shape and marker names in the form "{color} {fill} {shape}, marker {position}". For example, face `0` is "cyan solid circle, marker top". Face `64` is "cyan outline circle, marker top".

## Card states

- V14 - Give every hidden card the same back with a neutral diamond. Hidden cards keep their face artwork out of the DOM, as [Input](../interface/input.md#card-names) requires.
- V15 - Show the face artwork on revealed cards. Keep it shown on matched cards and add a Green palette border and check mark. Keep matched cards at full opacity.
- V16 - Show keyboard focus with a 3px white outline offset by 2px. Hover changes only the border to the Text color. Matched cards keep their Green border when hovered.
- V17 - Use a 120ms border-color transition. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, turn that transition off.

The gameplay document defines when card states change. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for turn timing and completion.

## Completion

- V18 - Show a win banner when the game finishes. Give it one 600ms pulse, then keep the banner static. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, show the static banner immediately. Use neither flashing nor confetti.

## Large boards

- V19 - At viewport sizes 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS pixels, render all 256 cards of a 16x16 board. Keep the page within the viewport width and keep controls reachable. Keep each card at least 44px square, with scrolling confined to the board when needed. Reach the first and last card by touch scrolling and by keyboard. Scroll focused cards fully into view without clipping their focus outline.

## Browser zoom

- V20 - At a 640x400 CSS-pixel viewport with device scale 2, the equivalent layout of 200% browser zoom from 1280x800, keep controls, status and the win summary readable without overlap. Keep the page within the viewport width. Keep both a 4x4 board and a 16x16 board playable with pointer and keyboard. Allow board scrolling and keep the focused card and its complete focus outline in view. Don't disable pinch zoom.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
---

# Sound
Sound is a game requirement that keeps Neon Pairs silent.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can play in a shared room without starting audio. Card feedback and completion are conveyed by the game display and accessible announcements.

## Playback

- S01 - Keep the game silent for every action and state, including a reveal, a match, a mismatch, a restart and a win.

- S02 - Include no audio files, audio API calls or sound toggle in this version. Silence is the required behavior, not an unfinished feature.

## Feedback

The game communicates card states and completion through its [visual design](../visuals/visuals.md). Turn results also use the [input announcements](../interface/input.md#announcements), so playing doesn't depend on hearing an event.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
---

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
---

# Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

item.aggregated_output:
## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes [ADR 011](adr-011-storage-keys.md). The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. [Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [Storage failure policy](../persistence/storage-failure-policy.md) describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs
3:  description: Preference validation, silent rejection and the timing of read
4:    rejection and later replacement.
11:This page explains how Neon Pairs handles unreadable or invalid stored data and how read rejection relates to a later save.
19:For current preferences, “empty” is the complete fallback `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }`. `DEFAULT_SIZE` is 4. The result is therefore a fresh default-size game with no known bests, rather than an empty board or a blocked screen. `readPreferences` makes that fallback before entering its `try` block and returns it from each rejection branch.
21:The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.
27:`isJsonObject` rejects null and arrays. After that narrowing, the reader checks `schemaVersion === PREFERENCES_VERSION` and requires `size` to have JavaScript type `number`. It then checks that size against `isValidSize` and requires `bestMoves` to be an object. A string value such as `"6"` is not accepted as a selected size even though the UI select ultimately uses string option values.
31:These branches are worth keeping separate in a test log. They converge on the same application state, but one shows absent data, another shows malformed syntax and another shows a structural mismatch. No error copy is rendered for these preference cases.
35:The reader builds a fresh `bestMoves` object and iterates through `Object.entries(value.bestMoves)`. For each entry it converts the key with `Number(size)`, then compares `String(numberSize)` with the original key. That round trip requires the canonical size spelling. It rejects `04`, `4.0`, `4e0` and strings padded with whitespace, even when numerical conversion would produce 4.
49:A failure at any entry returns the fallback for the entire preference value. A valid selected size of 6 does not survive alongside an invalid 4x4 score of 1. Likewise, valid score entries are not salvaged around one bad entry. The local object being assembled is never returned on that failure path.
51:This behavior is observable after reload: both the size preference and all previously accepted bests can appear reset when one map entry becomes invalid. It does not indicate that the size failed its own check. [Preferences store](preferences-store.md) explains why the aggregate is read as a unit.
67:This value has a valid map shape and an invalid key spelling:
79:All four produce the same preference fallback. The reader does not emit different messages or a machine-readable rejection reason. A diagnostic harness can identify the failed condition by choosing one changed field at a time. The production API does not expose those distinctions to components.
87:The 4x4 record is retained, the board starts at 6x6, and the 6x6 best display is `none`. Absence of a current-size best is not evidence of corruption.
93:This is different from the snapshot parser, which rejects unknown fields according to its own format. A shared JSON helper does not make all parsers equally strict. Tests that copy a snapshot rejection case into preferences without checking the reader could accidentally demand behavior the game does not implement.
95:The current reader also does not coerce score strings to numbers, round fractions or clamp out-of-range scores. A value of `"8"` is not accepted as a move count. A fraction is rejected rather than rounded. A number above the move cap invalidates the aggregate rather than being reduced to the cap. Validation produces a known state or the fallback, not a best-effort approximation of the edited input.
99:There are three useful points in a corruption test. Before initialization, the raw store contains the original text. After `readPreferences`, the caller has either accepted preferences or fallback preferences, and the raw store is still unchanged by that function. After `writePreferences`, the store may contain a valid serialized replacement if the write succeeded.
101:In the browser, those latter two stages are separated by React's render and effect cycle rather than by a player's explicit action. `useGame` initializes session state from the read result, then `useSavedPreferences` writes that state after mounting. A test inspecting storage only after the UI has settled can see valid defaults and miss the original corrupt text entirely.

docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:38:In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:42:There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.
docs/competition/competition-pairing.md:66:The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:28:`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:48:`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:50:Tournament match creation checks candidates against all codes already used in the event. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.
docs/competition/competition-deals.md:52:The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:41:The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.
docs/competition/competition-overview.md:49:The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:41:There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.
docs/competition/competition-scores.md:55:There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The tournament session keeps its own in-memory preferences and never connects them to the solo preference store, so those ordinary session updates do not alter the saved solo values.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:18:The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:34:`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.
docs/competition/competition-rounds.md:36:The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. Tournament controls render the round separately from the ordinary statistics.

item.aggregated_output:
## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

Tournament mode is implemented for four or eight players, with shared deals, knockout brackets, turn handoffs, champion display, local history, and JSON export and loading. Tournament results leave solo best scores and the saved solo board size unchanged.

Validation passed: the build, all 143 unit tests, and the targeted tournament, accessibility, and spacing browser tests. The broader browser run initially found keyboard-navigation and spacing failures; those checks passed after correction.

The repository-wide formatting check still reports pre-existing formatting issues in 210 files. The changed code and new tournament specification pass their targeted formatting check.
